splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries retain discretion to select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans flexibility in choosing the most current data for calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original expiration date.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term expires as originally set regardless of absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the separate requirements in § 2255(h). This determines how strictly federal prisoners are gatekept when bringing successive collateral attacks on their convictions.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim previously presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome determines whether candidates can challenge rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices before an election takes place.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge state election laws that allegedly affect the integrity or outcome of elections, including ballot-receipt deadlines.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not automatically have Article III standing to challenge state election rules pre-election without demonstrating concrete, particularized injury.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency interpretations (such as Auer/Kisor deference to Sentencing Commission commentary) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps agency deference in construing ambiguous criminal sentencing guidelines. At least three circuits hold lenity prevails, while the Third Circuit has held that agency deference trumps lenity. This split has deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron and raised questions about the continued viability of strong deference in criminal contexts.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal statutes or guidelines, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary interpretations prevails over the rule of lenity when the Guidelines text is ambiguous, allowing the Commission's anti-defendant reading to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Six circuits have split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one of the criteria is disqualifying. This split produces dramatically different sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit in which they are sentenced.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1, under Kisor v. Wilkie deference principles.
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor. Some circuits defer to the commentary and include inchoate offenses, while others find the guideline text unambiguously excludes them. The Commission has since amended the guideline text, but the split remains relevant for cases sentenced under prior versions.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative — inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2 is an authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson and Kisor, and therefore conspiracy qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Guideline text is unambiguous — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the plain text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously does not include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, and Application Note 1 cannot expand the guideline beyond its text under Kisor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can be considered as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that non-retroactive changes in law can never contribute to such a finding, while others and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) allow consideration of such changes. This affects large numbers of federal prisoners serving sentences under now-repealed mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may contribute to compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as one factor among others in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the underlying violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit has acknowledged an internal split and a broader circuit split on whether courts revoking supervised release may punish defendants for the conduct underlying their supervised release violation. This affects hundreds of individuals facing revocation proceedings each year and determines the permissible basis for revocation sentences.

positions.label: Courts may punish for underlying violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that at supervised release revocation, district courts may expressly consider and punish the defendant for the conduct constituting the supervised release violation.

positions.label: Revocation sentences must be based on breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that revocation of supervised release sanctions the defendant's breach of the court's trust, not the underlying criminal conduct, and sentences should reflect this distinction.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation inures to the estate, while other circuits have reached the opposite conclusion. This directly impacts debtors' ability to retain home equity when their Chapter 13 plans fail.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors, not the estate, particularly for good-faith conversions under § 348(f).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) includes state drug offenses involving substances not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines when the state criminalizes substances not on the federal schedule. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require the substance to be federally scheduled. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state offenses qualify
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled, finding no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal schedule required — must match federal law
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug offense qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance involved is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil time limit (30 days under FRAP 4(a)) or the criminal time limit (14 days under FRAP 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of the applicable appeal deadline. The majority view, joined by the Seventh Circuit, treats it as a civil matter with a 30-day deadline, while a minority applies the shorter 14-day criminal deadline. This affects the rights of acquitted or vindicated defendants seeking to recover legal costs.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and the 30-day civil appeal deadline under FRAP 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal proceeding and the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under FRAP 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the execution of their sentences (such as BOP decisions on prerelease custody and First Step Act time credits) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may alternatively bring civil rights claims.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions affecting the duration or conditions of their confinement, or whether civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) may also be available. This affects the procedural requirements and available relief for thousands of federal prisoners seeking to enforce First Step Act earned time credits and prerelease custody rights.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration challenges
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges decisions affecting the fact or duration of confinement, habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy and civil rights claims are barred.

positions.label: Civil rights claims may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights claims challenging conditions or execution of confinement even when habeas relief might also be available, particularly when the challenge relates to conditions rather than the core fact of confinement.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Carmona v. United States Bureau of Prisons

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
